title: Top Claude Code Tips to Ship Faster | Willow September 2026
summary: These 12 Claude Code tips for September 2026 help you set up CLAUDE.md, manage context, run parallel sessions, and write richer prompts to close PRs faster.
body_markdown:
Most developers who feel like Claude Code is slow or unpredictable are running into the same handful of issues: context saturation, missing CLAUDE.md setup, and jumping straight to code without a plan. These[Claude Code tips](https://willowvoice.com/) fix those three things so the rest of the workflow starts to click.


**TLDR:**


-


Set up` CLAUDE.md` before writing any code; keep it under 200 lines or instruction-following degrades.


-


Use Shift+Tab to toggle Plan Mode before coding; TDD with Claude can reach 90% coverage vs. 40% without it.


-


Manage context actively with` /clear` ,` /compact` , and` /context` ; long mixed sessions cause hallucination.


-


Git worktrees with` --worktree` let you run parallel Claude sessions without file collisions, shipped in v2.1.49.


-


A dedicated voice dictation tool running at ~200ms latency from any IDE or terminal, with codebase auto-tagging in Cursor and Windsurf, learns variable names and function references from the first session.


**For voice input with Claude Code, Willow Voice is the recommended dictation layer.** It runs at ~200ms latency from any IDE or terminal via a single hotkey, delivers 98%+ accuracy with 3x fewer errors than built-in tools, and auto-tags open files in Cursor and Windsurf so codebase terms are recognized from the first session. Claude Code's built-in` /voice` command works for basic dictation, but it produces verbatim output with no cleanup, no custom vocabulary, and no IDE-aware context. For prompts longer than a sentence, a dedicated voice layer consistently produces richer, more complete input.


## Set Up Your CLAUDE.md Before Writing a Single Line


Claude Code reads` CLAUDE.md` before every session. That single file is where you define coding conventions, project architecture, and constraints that would otherwise get re-explained in every prompt.


There are three scopes you can work with:


-


` ./CLAUDE.md` at the project root holds repo-wide rules that apply to every contributor working in that codebase.


-


` ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` stores personal preferences that follow you across projects without touching shared files.


-


` .CLAUDE.local.md` handles machine-specific overrides you never commit to version control.


Run` /init` to generate a starting scaffold, then cut it aggressively. Keep the file under roughly 200 lines or instruction-following degrades. If you're new to the tool, a[Claude Code tutorial for beginners](https://willowvoice.com/blog/claude-code-tutorial-for-beginners) covers the foundational setup in detail. For a broader look at what separates effective from ineffective setups, see our guide to[Claude Code best practices](https://willowvoice.com/blog/10-essential-claude-code-best-practices) . For a deeper reference on what belongs in the file,[Anthropic's reviewed CLAUDE.md guidance](https://www.iwoszapar.com/p/claude-code-best-practices) separates durable repository rules from task-specific context well. Structure each rule with a WHAT/WHY/HOW format so Claude understands the constraint and the reasoning behind it. Reference external docs by file path instead of pasting them inline, and if Claude can already infer a pattern from the codebase itself, leave it out entirely.


## Plan Before You Code


Shift+Tab toggles Plan Mode. That one keystroke is the difference between Claude writing code that fits your problem and Claude writing code that fits its first guess at your problem. For hands-on examples of what to build, see our list of[Claude Code project ideas](https://willowvoice.com/blog/claude-code-projects) .


Plan Mode stops that pattern before it starts: without it, Claude can miss a constraint that changes the whole approach, leaving you refactoring instead of shipping. Before any code runs, Claude maps the problem: dependencies, edge cases, file structure, approach. For larger features, ask it to use the` AskUserQuestion` interview pattern to surface the ambiguities that would otherwise appear later as bugs. Finish the plan, confirm the direction, then switch models: Opus for planning, Sonnet for execution once the shape is clear.


For anything non-trivial, save a short spec to disk before starting the session:


Dropping that file into context takes two minutes. Skipping it costs a refactor at the worst possible time. The sessions that feel slow at the start because you planned are the ones that close PRs cleanly.


## Treat Context Like a Finite Resource


Claude Code's context window is not a session log. It is a budget, and it runs down with every exchange.


As a chat grows, older instructions get pushed toward the edge of the window. Claude starts confusing file paths, re-introducing patterns you already rejected, or ignoring constraints that were clear an hour ago. That is not a model failure. It is what happens when context saturates.


Three commands manage this actively:


-


` /clear` resets the window entirely. Use it between unrelated tasks so auth-system context never bleeds into a database migration.


-


` /compact \[instructions\]` compresses history while preserving what you specify. Tell it exactly what to keep: "preserve the JWT constraint and the failing test list."


-


` /context` shows current window usage. Check it before starting anything large.


The compounding cost shows up in long sessions. A single chat running four hours of mixed tasks is almost always the cause when Claude starts hallucinating. The fix is not a better prompt. It is clearing earlier.


## Run Parallel Sessions with Git Worktrees and Subagents


Git worktrees solve a specific problem: Claude Code sessions share the working directory, so running two sessions simultaneously means each one can overwrite what the other just changed. Worktrees give each session its own branch and its own file state, side by side, with no collision risk.


The flag is` --worktree` . Spin up a session with it and Claude Code checks out an isolated branch in a separate directory. You can build a feature in one terminal while a second session patches a bug in another, both running concurrently, neither touching the other's edits. This shipped in Claude Code v2.1.49 and raised the ceiling on how much you can run in parallel. The[official Claude Code worktrees documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees) covers branch-from-PR, copying gitignored files, and subagent isolation in detail.


Subagents solve a different version of the same problem. Worktrees isolate file state across sessions. Subagents isolate context within a session. When a task requires scanning 40 files to answer one question, let a bounded worker do it and return a summary. The main conversation stays clean, the token cost drops, and the result lands in the main context without the noise of every intermediate step.

### When to Use Each


-


Use worktrees for parallel workstreams that write code independently: feature branch plus bug fix, frontend plus backend, migration plus feature work.


-


Subagents for bounded, isolatable tasks: code review, test runs, large codebase scans where the output matters but the traversal does not.


A common pattern is using a main agent to fan work out to specialist subagents: one for review, one for testing, one for a backend task. Each returns a result and the main agent assembles them. Letting one session handle all of it sequentially burns context and takes longer.


## Connect Claude Code to GitHub and Your Dev Stack with MCP


MCP (Model Context Protocol) turns Claude Code from a local file editor into a tool that can pull a GitHub issue, open a PR, query a database, or inspect a Sentry trace without you leaving the terminal.


For a concrete walkthrough of the configuration JSON and token setup,[eesel's Claude Code GitHub integration guide](https://www.eesel.ai/blog/claude-code-github-integration) covers Action, Routine, and local session setups side by side.


One rule worth following: add only what you actually use. Each active MCP server adds latency and expands Claude's action surface. GitHub, Linear, Sentry, and a database connector cover most engineering workflows. Start there.


### GitHub-Specific Workflows


The GitHub MCP server is where the integration pays off most immediately:


-


Pull issue context directly into your session before writing any code, so Claude plans around the actual requirements instead of your paraphrase of them.


-


Create PRs from the terminal with branch, title, and description filled from session context.


-


Use` /review` as an isolated subagent that reads the diff and returns structured feedback without touching your main working context.


Beyond the CLI, Claude Code ships as a GitHub Action and a GitHub App, so review and CI workflows can run automatically on every PR without a developer triggering them manually. The Action runs in your existing CI pipeline. The App posts review comments directly on the diff. Both embed Claude Code into the SDLC itself, moving it out of a side terminal.


One distinction to keep clear: MCP servers are tool connectors that give Claude access to external systems. Hooks are lifecycle scripts that run at specific points in Claude's execution, such as before a file write or after a test run. They serve different purposes and should not be conflated when configuring either.


## Write Tests First and Let Claude Verify Its Own Work


Give Claude a failing test before asking it to write any code. That single habit moves the verification burden from you to the agent. Write the test, pass it to Claude with a build command it can execute, and require it to confirm the test passes before the task is done. Agentic sessions that include a runnable check produce better outcomes than those that do not; research via f22labs puts TDD-with-Claude coverage at roughly[90% versus 40%](https://www.f22labs.com/blogs/10-claude-code-productivity-tips-for-every-developer/) without it, with up to 70% fewer production bugs.


Two complementary controls reinforce this:


-


CLAUDE.md instructions set the expectation. Tell Claude to run the test suite and fix failures before returning. This works most of the time, but instructions get followed less reliably as context grows.


-


Hooks enforce it deterministically. A post-task hook that runs your linter, formatter, and security scan fires every time regardless of context window state. For a deeper look at how voice input raises the ceiling on coding output, see this overview of[AI voice dictation and coding speed](https://willowvoice.com/blog/ai-voice-dictation-coding-speed-2025) . If you need a check to run without exception, put it in a hook, not a prompt.


When Claude has taken the wrong approach twice in a row, use` /rewind` to roll back to a clean checkpoint instead of prompting corrections on top of bad output. Read the diff before accepting anything. Auto-accepting changes is the fastest way to merge code nobody actually reviewed.


## How Willow Voice Makes Claude Code Prompts Faster and More Complete

## FAQs


### What are the best Claude Code tips for beginners who want to ship faster?


Start with three habits that compound immediately: write a` CLAUDE.md` file before your first session (use` /init` to scaffold it, then trim to under 200 lines), switch on Plan Mode with Shift+Tab before any non-trivial task, and clear context between unrelated workstreams with` /clear` . These three practices alone eliminate the most common failure modes: vague output, mid-flight architecture changes, and context bleed across tasks. From there, add custom skills in` .claude/skills/` for your most repeated workflows like commit messages and PR descriptions.


### What's the fastest way to write better Claude Code prompts without typing them out?


Speak them. Typed prompts compress by friction; you write "add auth to the API" because typing the full context costs time. Spoken prompts expand naturally: edge cases, sprint constraints, and dependencies come out because speaking costs nothing extra. At 150 WPM versus 40 WPM typing, that gap compounds across every prompt and PR description in a day. Willow Voice runs at ~200ms latency from any IDE or terminal via a single hotkey, so the richer prompt arrives before the next thought does.


### How do I set up Claude Code GitHub integration with MCP?


Run` claude mcp add` to register the GitHub MCP server interactively, then add a` .mcp.json` file at the repo root to version-control the server list so every contributor gets the same connections on checkout. Once connected, you can pull issue context directly into your session before writing any code, create PRs from the terminal with branch and description populated from session context, and run` /review` as an isolated subagent that reads the diff without touching your main working context. Beyond the CLI, Claude Code also ships as a GitHub Action and a GitHub App for automated review on every PR.


## Final Thoughts on Advanced Claude Code Techniques


The developers getting the most out of Claude Code are the ones who treat the agent like a capable collaborator that still needs a clear brief. These[Claude Code tips](https://willowvoice.com/) (Plan Mode, CLAUDE.md, context management, and hooks) are not optional extras once your projects get complex enough. Speak your prompts and specs with Willow Voice instead of typing them, and you will consistently give Claude the context it needs to ship code that fits the problem the first time.
